sections.title: 1. Options: Contract Characteristics & Mechanics
sections.overview: Options are derivative contracts granting the holder the right (not obligation) to buy (call) or sell (put) an underlying asset at a fixed strike price by expiration. Listed equity and index options are standardized, issued and guaranteed by the Options Clearing Corporation (OCC), and traded on registered exchanges. Mastery of contract terms, moneyness, premium components, and settlement timing is essential.
key_concepts: Call = right to BUY underlying at strike; Put = right to SELL underlying at strike.
Standard equity option contract = 100 shares of underlying.
Four key terms: underlying, strike (exercise) price, expiration date, premium.
American-style: exercisable any time before expiration (most equity options). European-style: exercisable only at expiration (most broad-based index options).
Settlement at exercise: equity options deliver stock (physical settlement); index options settle in CASH for intrinsic value the next business day.
Equity option premium settles next business day (T+1). Stock delivered upon exercise of an equity option settles T+1 (aligned with equity regular-way, effective 5/28/2024).
Moneyness — Call ITM: market > strike; Put ITM: market < strike; ATM: market = strike; OTM is the opposite.
Premium = Intrinsic Value + Time Value. Only ITM options have intrinsic value.
Long call/long put = holder (pays premium, has the right). Short call/short put = writer (receives premium, has the obligation).
Covered call = short call against long stock position. Uncovered (naked) = no offsetting position; unlimited risk on naked calls.
OCC is the issuer and guarantor of all listed options; OPRA disseminates option quotes.
Options Disclosure Document (ODD) — "Characteristics and Risks of Standardized Options" — must be delivered at or prior to approval of a customer's options account.
Uses: hedging (protective put, covered call), speculation (leverage), income (writing premium).
rules: Rule 2360 — defines options terms (call, class, series, aggregate exercise price), governs position/exercise limits, account approval, supervision, and customer disclosure standards for FINRA members transacting in standardized options.
OCC issues and guarantees all listed options (per Rule 2360 definitional framework).
Rule 1.1 (CBOE) — exchange-level definitions (e.g., ABBO) underpinning options market structure.
formulas: Aggregate Exercise Price = Strike Price × Number of Units (100 for equity options)
Call Intrinsic Value = max(0, Market Price − Strike)
Put Intrinsic Value = max(0, Strike − Market Price)
Premium = Intrinsic Value + Time Value
Long Call Breakeven = Strike + Premium
Long Put Breakeven = Strike − Premium
Long Call Max Loss = Premium paid; Max Gain = Unlimited
Long Put Max Loss = Premium paid; Max Gain = Strike − Premium (stock to zero)
Short (Naked) Call Max Gain = Premium; Max Loss = Unlimited
Short Put Max Gain = Premium; Max Loss = Strike − Premium
mnemonics: CALL UP / PUT DOWN — calls bullish, puts bearish for the holder.
OCC = One Central Clearer (issuer and guarantor).
PIPE: Premium = Intrinsic + Time, Expires worthless if OTM.
ODD before OK — Options Disclosure Document delivered before account approval.

sections.title: 2. Investment Company Act Classification (Packaged Products Framework)
sections.overview: The Investment Company Act of 1940 defines what an investment company is and classifies registered investment companies into three principal types, then subdivides management companies. This taxonomy is the legal backbone for mutual funds, closed-end funds, UITs, and ETFs.
key_concepts: Investment company (§3(a)): issuer primarily engaged in investing/reinvesting/trading in securities, OR holds >40% of total assets (ex Government securities and cash) in investment securities.
Three principal classes (§4): (1) Face-Amount Certificate Company; (2) Unit Investment Trust (UIT); (3) Management Company.
UIT (§4(2)): organized under trust indenture; NO board of directors; issues only REDEEMABLE securities representing undivided interest in a fixed portfolio.
Management companies (§5(a)) split into: Open-End (issues redeemable securities — mutual funds, open-end ETFs) and Closed-End (any management company that is not open-end).
Further subdivision (§5(b)) — Diversified vs. Non-Diversified.

Diversified Company (75-5-10 test): at least 75% of total assets in cash/cash items, Government securities, securities of other investment companies, and other securities limited per issuer to ≤5% of total assets AND ≤10% of issuer's outstanding voting securities.
Non-diversified: any management company not meeting the 75-5-10 test.
rules: Investment Company Act of 1940 §3(a) — definition of "investment company"; 40% asset test.
Investment Company Act of 1940 §4 — three classes: face-amount certificate, UIT, management company.
Investment Company Act of 1940 §5 — open-end vs. closed-end; diversified vs. non-diversified (75-5-10).
17 CFR 270.12b-1 — permits open-end funds to use fund assets to pay distribution/marketing expenses under a written 12b-1 plan.
formulas: Diversified test (per §5(b)(1)): 75% of assets where, within that 75%, any single issuer ≤ 5% of total assets AND ≤ 10% of issuer's voting securities.
Investment company threshold (§3(a)(1)(C)): Investment securities > 40% × (Total Assets − Government securities − Cash items)
mnemonics: F-U-M: Face-amount, UIT, Management (the three §4 classes).
75-5-10 = Diversified.
UIT = Unmanaged, Undivided, Unit redeemable (no board, fixed portfolio).

sections.title: 3. Open-End Funds (Mutual Funds) — Pricing, Loads, Share Classes
sections.overview: Open-end management companies continuously issue and redeem shares at NAV (forward-priced). They are sold by prospectus and may charge front-end, back-end, or asset-based distribution fees. Breakpoints and aggregation rules reduce sales charges for larger investments.
key_concepts: NAV = (Total Fund Assets − Liabilities) / Shares Outstanding; calculated at least once per business day.
Forward pricing — orders execute at the next computed NAV.
Public Offering Price (POP) = NAV + Sales Charge (for front-load funds).
Share Classes: Class A (front-end load, lower 12b-1), Class B (back-end CDSC, higher 12b-1; often convert to A), Class C (level load, ongoing 12b-1, small/no CDSC).
12b-1 Fee — asset-based annual distribution/service fee under Rule 12b-1 plan.
Breakpoints — discounts on sales charges at specified investment levels.
Letter of Intent (LOI) — non-binding statement to invest enough within 13 months to reach a breakpoint; may be backdated up to 90 days.
Right of Accumulation (ROA) — prior holdings count toward breakpoints on new purchases.
Breakpoint sale — selling shares just below a breakpoint to share in higher commissions is prohibited (Rule 2342).
Redemption — fund must redeem within 7 days of request (Investment Company Act).
Net transaction — disclosed transaction with no commission added; price reflects markup/markdown.
rules: 17 CFR 270.12b-1 — distribution fees from fund assets allowed only under a written plan approved by board and shareholders.
Rule 2342 — prohibits sales just below breakpoints designed to capture higher sales charges; bona fide asset-allocation programs are an exception with proper disclosure.
Investment Company Act of 1940 §5(a)(1) — open-end company defined by issuing redeemable securities.
formulas: NAV per share = (Assets − Liabilities) / Shares Outstanding
POP = NAV / (1 − Sales Charge %)
Sales Charge % = (POP − NAV) / POP
Sales Charge $ = POP − NAV
mnemonics: ABC of share classes: A=front, B=back, C=continuous (level).
LOI = 13 months forward, 90 days back.
Forward pricing: "Order today, NAV tonight."

sections.title: 4. Closed-End Funds, UITs, and ETPs (ETFs/ETNs)
sections.overview: Closed-end funds and UITs are non-redeemable from the investor's standpoint and trade or are traded differently than mutual funds. ETPs include ETFs (registered investment companies) and ETNs (unsecured debt). Spot Bitcoin ETPs were SEC-approved 1/10/2024 and spot Ether ETPs on 5/23/2024.
key_concepts: Closed-End Fund (CEF): fixed number of shares issued in IPO; trades intraday on exchange at market price that may be at premium or discount to NAV; not redeemable with issuer.
UIT: fixed portfolio; units redeemable with the trust; no active management; terminates on a specified date; no board of directors.

ETF: typically open-end fund (or UIT structure); trades intraday on exchange; uses creation/redemption mechanism via Authorized Participants to keep price near NAV; generally passive (index-tracking) but actively managed ETFs exist.
ETN: senior unsecured DEBT obligation of issuing bank; tracks an index; carries CREDIT RISK of issuer; not an investment company.
Fee considerations: ETFs typically have lower expense ratios than comparable mutual funds; investors also pay brokerage commissions/spreads.
Spot Bitcoin ETPs approved 1/10/2024; spot Ether ETPs approved 5/23/2024.
Active vs. passive — passive tracks an index; active seeks to outperform a benchmark.
rules: Investment Company Act of 1940 §4(2) — UIT defined (no board, redeemable undivided interest, trust indenture).
Investment Company Act of 1940 §5(a)(2) — Closed-end management company definition.
17 CFR 270.12b-1 — applies to open-end ETFs' distribution fees.
formulas: CEF Premium/Discount % = (Market Price − NAV) / NAV × 100
ETF Tracking Error = Std. Deviation of (ETF Return − Index Return)
mnemonics: ETN = Equity-linked, Treated as Note (credit risk).
CEF: Closed, Exchange-traded, Fixed shares.
UIT: Unmanaged, Indenture-based, Terminates.

sections.title: 5. Variable Annuities and Variable Contracts
sections.overview: Variable annuities are insurance/securities hybrid products providing tax-deferred growth and optional annuitization. Subaccounts function like mutual funds and bear investment risk on the contract holder. Recommendations are governed by FINRA Rule 2330 with heightened suitability and supervisory review.
key_concepts: Two phases: Accumulation (units purchased, value fluctuates) and Annuitization/Payout (units converted to annuity units; periodic payments).
Tax: tax-deferred growth inside contract; ordinary income on earnings at withdrawal; 10% penalty on withdrawals before age 59½.
Surrender charges: contingent deferred sales charges typically declining over a multi-year schedule.
Mortality & Expense (M&E) risk charge — covers insurance guarantees.
Death benefit (minimum return of premium or stepped-up value) and optional living benefits (GMIB, GMWB) via riders.
Subaccount allocation and exchanges (1035 exchanges) require special scrutiny.
Required disclosures: surrender period/charge, tax penalty, M&E fees, advisory fees, rider charges, market risk, insurance + investment components.
rules: Rule 2330 — applies to recommended purchases/exchanges of deferred variable annuities and initial subaccount allocations; requires reasonable basis to believe (a) customer is informed of key features (surrender, tax penalty, M&E, riders, market risk); (b) customer would benefit from features (tax deferral, annuitization, death/living benefits); (c) the specific contract and subaccounts are suitable; for exchanges, must consider new surrender period, lost benefits, and prior exchanges within 36 months.
Registered principal review of variable annuity applications required under Rule 2330.
formulas: Tax on non-qualified VA withdrawal: Earnings withdrawn first (LIFO) taxed as ordinary income; 10% additional tax if before 59½.
mnemonics: VA Risks SAID: Surrender, Annuitization is irrevocable, Insurance fees, Deferred tax (penalty if early).
2330 = Triple-Three suitability: Informed, Benefitted, Suitable.

sections.title: 6. Municipal Fund Securities (529 Plans, LGIPs, ABLE)
sections.overview: Municipal fund securities are issued by entities that would be investment companies but for §2(b) of the Investment Company Act and are regulated by the MSRB. They include 529 college savings plans, prepaid tuition plans, LGIPs, and ABLE accounts.
key_concepts: 529 Savings Plan: state-sponsored; contributions grow federal tax-deferred; qualified distributions (qualified education expenses, K-12 tuition up to limits, student loan repayments) federally tax-free; donor retains control; beneficiary changeable within family.
529 Prepaid Tuition Plan: locks in future tuition at today's prices; typically state residency requirements; usually limited to tuition/fees.

529-to-Roth IRA Rollover (SECURE 2.0, effective 2024): tax- and penalty-free rollover subject to $35,000 lifetime cap, 15-year-old account requirement, and annual rollover capped at IRA contribution limit.
Owner vs. Beneficiary: account owner controls assets and distributions; beneficiary is the student.
LGIPs (Local Government Investment Pools): investment pools for state/local government entities; not for retail investors; provide cash-management-like vehicle.
ABLE Accounts (529A): tax-advantaged savings for individuals with disabilities (onset before age 26, rising to 46 in 2026 under SECURE 2.0); qualified disability expenses tax-free.
Direct-sold vs. adviser-sold 529 plans — adviser-sold typically have sales charges/loads; direct-sold typically lower cost.
Tax advantage outside the home state — investors may lose state tax deduction by investing in out-of-state plan (must disclose).
rules: Rule D-12 — defines "Municipal Fund Security" as a municipal security issued by an issuer that, but for §2(b) of the Investment Company Act, would be an investment company under §3.
Rule G-17 — fair-dealing standard applicable to municipal securities dealers, including 529/ABLE distributions.
Rule G-45 — periodic reporting on 529 and ABLE program data to the MSRB.
Investment Company Act of 1940 §3(a) — referenced by Rule D-12.
formulas: 529-to-Roth rollover cap = $35,000 lifetime (subject to annual IRA contribution limit and 15-year account-age requirement).
mnemonics: 529 OWNER controls, BENEFICIARY uses.
D-12 = Defines (Municipal Fund Security).
G-45 = reGulatory data filing for 529s.

sections.title: 7. Direct Participation Programs (DPPs)
sections.overview: DPPs are non-corporate entities providing flow-through (pass-through) tax treatment to investors, most commonly structured as limited partnerships. They are generally illiquid, unlisted, and require heightened suitability review.
key_concepts: Flow-through taxation: income, gains, losses, deductions, and credits pass through to investors (no entity-level federal income tax).
Structure: General Partner (GP) manages, has unlimited liability and fiduciary duty; Limited Partners (LPs) are passive investors with liability limited to investment.
Tenants-in-Common (TIC): co-ownership structure used in real estate DPPs.
Typical DPPs: oil & gas (exploratory, developmental, income), real estate (raw land, new construction, existing properties, government-assisted), equipment leasing, agricultural.
Excluded from DPP definition (Rule 2310): REITs, qualified retirement plans (401, 403(a), 408 IRAs, 403(b)), and registered investment companies.
Risks: ILLIQUIDITY (no active secondary market), tax-law risk, GP management risk, capital risk, recapture.
Cash flow vs. cash available for distribution — distinct measures (G-30/Rule 2310 definitions).
Subscription agreement — required for investor admission; GP/sponsor evaluates suitability.
rules: Rule 2310 — governs FINRA members' participation in public DPP offerings: definitions, suitability inquiry, organization-and-offering expenses, GP/sponsor affiliations, and compensation limits; defines DPP, affiliate, cash flow, cash available for distribution.
DPP definition (Rule 2310(a)(4)) — flow-through tax consequences regardless of entity form; expressly excludes REITs, qualified plans, and registered investment companies.
formulas: Cash Available for Distribution = Cash Flow − Reserves
Cash Flow (Rule 2310) = Operating cash receipts − operating cash expenses − debt service − capital improvements/replacements (before depreciation)
mnemonics: DPP = Don't Pay (entity) tax; Pass-through, Partnership, Possibly illiquid.
LP = Limited liability, Passive role.
GP = General liability, Generally manages.

sections.title: 8. Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs)
sections.overview: REITs pool capital to invest in real estate equity or mortgage debt and pass income through to shareholders without entity-level federal tax, provided they meet IRC qualification requirements. They are distinct from DPPs because losses do NOT pass through.
key_concepts: Tax qualification (general industry rule): distribute at least 90% of taxable income to shareholders; at least 75% of assets in real estate; at least 75% of gross income from real estate sources.
No double taxation on distributed income; dividends taxed as ordinary income to shareholders (no pass-through of losses — distinguishing from DPPs).
Types by structure: Listed (exchange-traded — liquid), Public Non-Listed (PNLR — registered with SEC, not exchange-traded, illiquid), Private (unregistered, only for accredited investors).
Types by holdings: Equity REIT (owns income-producing property), Mortgage REIT (originates/holds real-estate debt; sensitive to interest rates), Hybrid.
Risks: interest-rate risk (especially mortgage REITs), real estate market risk, liquidity risk (non-listed).
Excluded from DPP definition under Rule 2310.
rules: Rule 2310 — explicitly excludes REITs from the DPP definition.
Securities Act of 1933 — public non-listed REIT offerings require registration and prospectus delivery.
formulas: REIT qualification rule of thumb: 90% income distributed / 75% real estate assets / 75% real estate gross income.
mnemonics: REIT = Real Estate Income, Tax-advantaged (no double tax, but no loss pass-through).
90-75-75 — distribution / assets / income tests.

sections.title: 9. Hedge Funds and Private Funds
sections.overview: Hedge funds are pooled, privately offered investment vehicles typically structured as limited partnerships and exempt from Investment Company Act registration under §3(c)(1) or §3(c)(7). They employ flexible strategies and are sold only to qualified investors.
key_concepts: Structure: limited partnership or LLC; manager is GP/managing member; investors are LPs.
Exemptions used: ICA §3(c)(1) (≤100 beneficial owners) or §3(c)(7) (sold only to qualified purchasers).
Investors: accredited investors / qualified purchasers; high minimum investments.
Liquidity: ILLIQUID — lock-up periods, redemption gates, quarterly/annual redemption windows.
Fee structure: typically "2 and 20" — 2% management fee + 20% performance/incentive fee, often subject to hurdle rate and high-water mark.
Strategies: long/short equity, global macro, arbitrage, event-driven, distressed.
Private equity funds — similar private-fund structure; invest in non-public companies; very long lock-ups (often 7–10+ years).
Risks: leverage, illiquidity, lack of transparency, manager risk, valuation risk.
rules: Investment Company Act §3(c)(1) and §3(c)(7) — exclusions from investment company definition under which hedge funds rely.
Investment Company Act of 1940 §3(a) — definitional baseline.
formulas: Performance Fee = Performance % × (Return − Hurdle Rate) × NAV above High-Water Mark
"2 and 20" annual cost ≈ 2% × NAV + 20% × Profit above hurdle/HWM
mnemonics: Hedge Fund HALL: High minimums, Accredited investors, Lock-ups, Limited partnership.
3(c)(1) = 100 owners; 3(c)(7) = Qualified purchasers.

sections.title: 10. Investment Risks: Identification and Mitigation
sections.overview: Representatives must identify the distinct risks attached to each product and recommend mitigation strategies aligned to client objectives. The SIE outline enumerates specific risk types and three primary mitigation tools.
key_concepts: Capital Risk — loss of principal invested.
Credit (Default) Risk — issuer fails to pay interest/principal (corporate/muni bonds, ETNs).
Currency (Exchange Rate) Risk — adverse FX moves affecting foreign securities/ADRs.
Inflation / Purchasing Power Risk — fixed payments lose real value; primary risk for long-term fixed-income.
Interest Rate Risk — bond prices fall as rates rise; longer duration = greater sensitivity.
Reinvestment Risk — cash flows reinvested at lower rates; significant for callable bonds and MBS.
Liquidity (Marketability) Risk — inability to sell quickly without price concession (DPPs, non-listed REITs, hedge funds, private placements).
Market / Systematic Risk — broad market decline; cannot be diversified away.
Non-Systematic (Business/Unsystematic) Risk — company- or industry-specific; can be diversified away.
Political / Legislative Risk — government action, tax law changes, sovereign actions.
Prepayment Risk — borrowers prepay mortgages when rates fall (MBS, CMOs); a form of reinvestment risk.
Mitigation tools: Diversification (reduces non-systematic risk), Portfolio Rebalancing (restore target allocation), Hedging (offsetting positions — e.g., protective puts, short futures).
rules: Rule 2261 — member must make balance sheet (financial condition) available to bona fide customers on request (relevant to assessing counterparty/credit risk of a member).
Rule 2262 — disclosure of control relationship between member and issuer before transaction (mitigates conflict-of-interest risk).
Rule G-30 — fair-pricing/markup standard for municipal securities, including PMP "waterfall" analysis (mitigates pricing risk to customers).
formulas: Total Risk = Systematic Risk + Non-Systematic Risk
Only non-systematic risk is reduced by diversification.
Duration ≈ % change in bond price for a 1% change in interest rates.
mnemonics: CCC-LIMP-PR: Capital, Credit, Currency, Liquidity, Inflation, Market, Political, Prepayment, Reinvestment.
DRH = Diversify, Rebalance, Hedge.
Systematic = STays (cannot diversify); Non-Systematic = Negated by diversification.

sections.title: 11. Cross-Cutting Disclosure & Conduct Rules for Other Investment Vehicles
sections.overview: Several SRO rules cut across packaged products, options, DPPs, and municipal fund securities to ensure suitability, fair pricing, and required disclosures.
key_concepts: Financial condition disclosure to customers on request (Rule 2261).
Control relationship between member and issuer must be disclosed before transacting (Rule 2262).
DPP organizational, compensation, and suitability requirements (Rule 2310).
Deferred variable annuity recommendation/principal review (Rule 2330).
Breakpoint sales prohibition for mutual fund shares (Rule 2342).
Standardized options conduct, account approval, ODD delivery, position limits (Rule 2360).
Municipal Fund Security definition (Rule D-12).
Fair-dealing and disclosure for municipal securities, including 529s (Rule G-17).
Prevailing Market Price determination and markup discipline for municipal securities (Rule G-30 with "waterfall" SM .06).
Periodic 529/ABLE program data reporting (Rule G-45).
Issuer share repurchase safe harbor — Rule 10b-18 (relevant to corporate equity market conduct).
Equity security definition — 17 CFR 240.3a11-1.
rules: Rule 2261 — Disclosure of Financial Condition upon customer request.
Rule 2262 — Disclosure of Control Relationship with issuer before transaction.
Rule 2310 — Direct Participation Programs conduct standards.
Rule 2330 — Members' Responsibilities Regarding Deferred Variable Annuities (suitability, principal review, exchange considerations).
Rule 2342 — Prohibition on "Breakpoint Sales."
Rule 2360 — Standardized options conduct, definitions, supervision.
Rule D-12 (MSRB) — Municipal Fund Security definition.
Rule G-17 (MSRB) — Conduct of municipal securities activities; fair dealing.
Rule G-30 (MSRB) — Prices and commissions; PMP waterfall.
Rule G-45 (MSRB) — Reporting of information on municipal fund securities (529/ABLE).
17 CFR 240.10b-18 — Safe harbor for issuer repurchases of equity securities.
17 CFR 240.3a11-1 — Definition of "equity security."
mnemonics: "Disclose Before You Close" — Rule 2262 control relationships disclosed before transaction.
G-Rules for Munis: G-17 (Fair), G-30 (Price), G-45 (Filing).
